The letter folded against her stays could shorten that to nothing, or end her entirely.

The letter was from her brother Declan in Cork, who had finally scraped together passage money. But Mairead could not simply walk away from the Pemberton house: her indenture was a legal bond, and the constables collected runaways for a shilling a head. What she needed was the bond-paper itself, locked in Mr. Pemberton's bureau, struck through with ink to mark her freed.

Which was why she had sent word to Tobias Ackland, the underclerk who kept the household ledgers.

He came round the corner now, hat pulled low, breath visible in the cold. He was twenty-three, thin, with the careful eyes of a man who had risen one rung and meant to climb another. Mairead had been kind to him during his fevers last winter—broth, a stolen orange—and he had once said, half-drunk on small beer at Michaelmas, that he was in her debt.

"You've considered it?" she asked.

"I have the key copied," Tobias said. "I can strike the bond tonight. Mr. Pemberton won't open that drawer again until quarter-day. By then you'll be on the Cork packet."

She studied his face. He could do exactly as promised. Or he could go straight to Pemberton with her letter as proof of intent to abscond—a service that would surely earn him the chief clerkship Pemberton had been dangling. He would be made for life.

"And what do you want for it?" she said.

"Nothing you have not already given me." He would not meet her eyes when he said it.

She had to decide now, on this quay, in this wind. To hand him the letter and walk back to the house pretending nothing was changed, trusting him to scratch out her name in the dark. Or to burn the letter in the cooperage furnace, finish her eleven months scrubbing flagstones, and reach Declan a free woman through the slow lawful door.

Here was the shape of it. If she trusted Tobias and he kept faith, she would be aboard the packet within a fortnight, reunited with the only family she had left—a future worth, by her own reckoning, a hundred guineas of life. If she trusted him and he betrayed her, she would be whipped at the cart's tail, her indenture doubled, perhaps transported to Virginia—everything lost. If she chose instead to wait out her bond honestly, she would still have her freedom in eleven months, plain and small, worth perhaps five guineas of bread and a Cork lodging. Tobias, for his part, stood to gain a clerkship worth far more than the orange she had once slipped him, should he sell her out.
